title: Greater certainty, greater investment: the value of spectrum continuity
summary: Find out more about Greater certainty, greater investment: the value of spectrum continuity, don't miss it.
body_markdown:
In the middle of this year, we published a[Policy Brief](https://www.telefonica.com/en/wp-content/uploads/sites/5/2026/06/digital-networks-act-policy-brief-2026.pdf) setting out Telefónica’s perspective on the European Commission’s[Digital Networks Act proposal](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/proposal-regulation-digital-networks-act-dna) (DNA). The publication was accompanied by the launch of a series of posts on our blog exploring the aspects of the proposal we consider most important.


This post builds on our DNA[series](https://www.telefonica.com/en/tag/digital-networks-act/) , particularly the article on[spectrum policy](https://www.telefonica.com/en/communication-room/blog/spectrum-rules-dna-matter-europes-digital-future/) , in light of developments in the legislative process. It focuses on an issue that is vital to the sector and that we hope will be retained in the final text adopted by the co-legislators: spectrum licences.


## The Commission’s recognition of indefinite licences and automatic renewals


The Commission’s provisions on spectrum were a particularly positive element of the proposal, including a shift towards indefinite-duration licences and automatic renewal as the default.


It is essential to maintain the direction set out for spectrum policy by supporting longer licence terms and automatic, predictable renewals. One area for improvement is the introduction of appropriate transitional provisions so that licences expiring during the transition period, before the new regulation becomes fully applicable, can benefit from the new framework and avoid unnecessary uncertainty.


## Why does extending spectrum licences matter?


Mobile networks are deployed over long investment cycles, and spectrum is one of their essential resources. Network rollouts require long-term decisions made several years in advance. Ensuring continued access to spectrum through renewal processes is therefore crucial to providing investment certainty.


Renewals enable mobile operators to plan future investment, build confidence amonginvestors and maintain stable operations. This ensures access to the spectrum needed to deliver connectivity to millions of consumers and businesses while supporting the next wave of innovation.


Furthermore, extending licences can reduce operators’ spectrum-related expenditure, freeing up additional resources for network investment.[GSMA](https://www.gsmaintelligence.com/research/mobile-investment-needs-in-europe) estimates that the certainty provided by licence renewals could stimulate investment in mobile infrastructure, increasing network speeds by up to 23% and adding up to €75 billion to European GDP by 2035.


## Indefinite or long-term licences do not mean unrestricted spectrum rights or less competition


Indefinite licences do not constrain regulators’ ability to act. Regulatory powers to enforce licence conditions remain fully intact. Nor do indefinite-duration licences undermine effective and sustainable market competition, particularly where spectrum is used efficiently.


First, indefinite-duration licences do not remove regulatory oversight of spectrum. Authorities retain their powers to ensure that this resource is used efficiently and, where appropriate, to revoke a licence if the spectrum is not being used effectively. Second, indefinite licences do not inherently create barriers to entry or to competition, including the existence of secondary spectrum markets. In practice, the current system of time-limited licences has not demonstrated that non-renewal is an effective mechanism for facilitating the entry of new operators.


In competitive markets, operators have strong commercial incentives to provide wholesale accesssince it creates additional revenue opportunities. Indeed, competition in terrestrial mobile networks helps explain why ex ante wholesale access regulation has progressively been scaled back, with EU-level regulation withdrawn in 2007. And new players may also enter by accessing other spectrum bands made available to meet emerging demand and technological needs.


Finally, there is no evidence that holding new auctions instead of renewals results in the effective reallocation of spectrum to new players. An October 2026 report by[Cullen](https://wwworigin.cullen-international.com/news/2026/10/What-European-spectrum-regulators-do-when-licences-are-about-to-expire.html) International shows that, among the 21 countries analysed, ten hold new auctions, seven use mixed approaches combining auctions and renewals, and only four opt for renewal alone. Yet even when spectrum already in use is auctioned again, it is rarely reassigned to a new entrant, and the outcomes have been far from satisfactory.


## The risks of auctions versus renewals: the case of Norway


The few instances in which spectrum already in use has been reassigned to a new entrant through a competitive auction, to foster competition but with a focus on maximising auction prices, have had particularly negative consequences.


The case of Tele2 in Norway is illustrative. Following a new spectrum auction, the operator lost access to the frequencies it needed to provide services on viable terms. Those frequencies were awarded to its competitors and a new entrant, Telco Data (later ICE). This ultimately undermined Tele2’s ability to continue operating, leading it to sell its Norwegian operations to TeliaSonera in 2014–2015. The entry of a new player did not offset the departure of an established network operator. Although Telco Data obtained spectrum, it did not replace Tele2’s competitive role in the short term. Indeed, the Norwegian competition authority identified the risk of the market shrinking from three to two mobile network operators and required specific remedies to preserve a three-operator market structure.


To sum up, spectrum reallocation does not guarantee greater competition and may have the opposite effect. Predictable renewal of existing rights supports stability, investment and the continuity of competition.


## The United Kingdom and Spain: European benchmarks in spectrum policy


The United Kingdom and Spain have been pioneers in recognising the benefits of longer spectrum licence terms as a means of encouraging investment and developing their connectivity ecosystems.


In 2010, the United Kingdom introduced[indefinite-duration spectrum licences](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukdsi/2010/9780111497319/data.html) for certain uses through a 2010 order under the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006, with the aim, among others, of “providing greater certainty for operators’ investments”. This new approach to UK spectrum policy reflected the need to ensure that spectrum availability did not become an obstacle to releasing its economic and social potential. The reform placed the United Kingdom at the forefront of innovation in spectrum management and remains in force today, without having produced adverse outcomes or undermined competition.


In 2024, pursuant to the 2022 General Telecommunications Act, Spain[extended](https://digital.gob.es/content/dam/portal-mtdfp/comunicacion/comunicacion_setid/2024/06/2024-06-20/20240620_NdP_Extension_de_licencias_del_espectro.pdf) certain spectrum concessions granted before that act, which had increased the maximum concession term to 40 years. Spain awarded the 700 MHz and 26 GHz bands under 20-year licences that can be extended by up to a further 20 years, subject to compliance with the conditions attached to each authorisation. The government presented the measure as part of its strategy to “provide greater consistency and sustainability for the sector” and redirect resources towards network deployment and innovation for the benefit of society.


## Towards a new investment-oriented spectrum framework


The European Union is moving in the right direction by promoting greater certainty and continuity of spectrum access as part of the legislative debate on the DNA. This is essential to preserve the value of operators’ existing investments and avoid unnecessary reallocation of spectrum that is already being used efficiently. In practice, the likelihood of attracting a new investor in these circumstances is limited, while the risk of disrupting existing services and weakening incentives for continued network investment is considerable.


The examples of Spain and the United Kingdom show how a long-term spectrum policy can be used strategically to give operators greater predictability and encourage connectivity investment. By contrast, Norway illustrates the risks arising from uncertainty over licence continuity and its impact on operators’ ability to plan investment and maintain their market position. Ultimately, Europe needs a stable and predictable spectrum framework that gives operators the certainty required to invest for the long term. This will create the conditions needed to accelerate network deployment and strengthen Europe’s competitiveness in connectivity.
